Empirical Research Plan  
“Does corporate governance quality affect acquirer announcement-period returns?”

======================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred strategy: 2-stage least squares (2SLS) using exogenous state-level anti-takeover law changes as instruments for the firm-level Governance Index (G-index or E-index).

Why IV?  
• The raw correlation between governance and CARs is plausibly confounded by unobservable managerial talent, investment opportunities, or corporate culture; governance is chosen, not randomly assigned.  
• Between 1982 and 1991 U.S. states adopted three major anti-takeover statutes—Control-Share Acquisition (CSA) laws, Business-Combination (BC) laws, and Fair-Price (FP) laws—at different calendar years. For firms incorporated in a given state, the passage of a new statute makes it mechanically easier and cheaper to adopt the corresponding corporate-charter provisions (poison pills, fair-price amendments, supermajority rules, …).  
• The staggered timing across states provides plausibly exogenous variation that predicts a higher number of ATPs but is orthogonal to an individual firm’s subsequent acquisition decisions and announcement-period returns, conditional on rich fixed effects and controls.

Econometric specification  
First stage (relevance):  
G_index_{ist} = α + β₁ CSA_{st} + β₂ BC_{st} + β₃ FP_{st} + γX_{it−1}+ ϕ_i + δ_t + ε_{ist}

Second stage (causal effect):  
CAR_{it} = θ Ĝ_index_{ist} + λX_{it−1} + ϕ_i + δ_t + η_{it}

where  
• s = incorporating state, i = firm, t = acquisition-announcement year  
• X = firm controls and deal controls  
• ϕ_i  = firm fixed effects (absorbing time-invariant unobservables)  
• δ_t  = calendar-year fixed effects (absorbing aggregate shocks)

Parallel analyses:  
(i) treat governance as a continuous index; (ii) a binary treatment “high entrenchment” (G ≥ 14 or E ≥ 3) estimated with linear probability first stage and 2SLS/LIML; (iii) OLS with rich fixed effects as a robustness baseline.

======================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Continuous: G_index (0–24) or E_index (0–6)—higher = weaker shareholder rights.  
• Binary: High_Entrenchment = 1{G_index ≥ 14} (upper quartile).

Control group / counterfactual  
• Firms with low or moderate entrenchment (G < 14) serve as the comparison set.  
• With firm fixed effects the practical counterfactual for a treated observation is the same firm in years in which its governance index is lower.

Timing / variation  
• “Treatment” is measured as of the last IRRC publication preceding the acquisition announcement (to avoid post-treatment measurement).  
• Exogenous variation arises from the year a state adopts a new ATP statute.

======================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 (Relevance): State ATP statutes increase the propensity to adopt firm-level ATPs. – Empirically well documented; first-stage F-stat > 10 expected.

A2 (Exclusion): Conditional on firm, industry, and year fixed effects plus controls, state ATP statutes affect acquirer CARs only through their impact on the firm’s governance provisions, not through any other channel. – Plausible because statutes govern takeover defenses, not operating performance; remaining concerns handled in section 4.

A3 (Stable Unit Treatment): A statute in state s does not directly change governance of firms incorporated in other states. – Reasonable given corporate law jurisdiction.

A4 (No differential pre-trends): In absence of governance changes, CAR trends for firms in states about to adopt a statute would parallel those in states that never adopt. – Can be inspected with event-study leads.

======================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Policy endogeneity: States might pass ATP laws because local firms face unique takeover waves that also influence CARs.  
  Mitigation:  
  • Include state-specific linear time trends and state×industry employment growth controls.  
  • Conduct placebo tests using leads (laws 3–5 years before adoption should not predict governance nor CARs).

2. Measurement error in G (IRRC snapshots every 2–3 years).  
  Mitigation:  
  • Use closest pre-deal snapshot only.  
  • Instrument alleviates attenuation bias; robustness dropping deals >18 months from a snapshot.

3. Sample selection: We only observe completed deals >$1 m; firms with poor governance might attempt and abandon more deals.  
  Mitigation:  
  • Compare announcement CARs of withdrawn deals (where available).  
  • Heckman selection model with probit first stage (announce vs. no announce) as sensitivity.

======================================================================
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effect estimators incl. IV
library(ivreg)       # for classic 2SLS robustness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
car      <- read_csv("crsp_cars.csv")          # CAR[-1,+1] per deal_id
sdc      <- read_csv("sdc_deals.csv")          # deal characteristics
govern   <- read_csv("irrc_governance.csv")    # G_index, E_index by firm-year
comp     <- read_csv("compustat_fundamentals.csv")
laws     <- read_csv("state_atp_laws.csv")     # CSA, BC, FP adoption years
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge and construct variables
data <- sdc %>% 
  left_join(car,  by = "deal_id") %>% 
  left_join(govern, by = c("gvkey", "fyear")) %>%       # fyear = last pre-deal fiscal year
  left_join(comp,  by = c("gvkey", "fyear")) %>% 
  left_join(laws,  by = c("inc_state", "year" = "adopt_year")) %>% 
  mutate(
    high_entrench = as.integer(G_index >= 14),
    log_assets    = log(at_assets),
    rel_size      = deal_value / at_assets,
    cash_pct      = cash_and_eq / at_assets,
    qhat          = tobins_q,
    tender        = as.integer(deal_structure == "Tender Offer"),
    stock_pay     = as.integer(payment == "Stock"),
    law_CSA       = as.integer(year >= CSA_year & !is.na(CSA_year)),
    law_BC        = as.integer(year >= BC_year  & !is.na(BC_year)),
    law_FP        = as.integer(year >= FP_year  & !is.na(FP_year))
  ) %>%
  drop_na(CAR, G_index)   # keep complete cases

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main 2SLS specification
iv_main <- feols(CAR ~ 1 | gvkey + year | 
                   (G_index ~ law_CSA + law_BC + law_FP) , 
                 data = data,
                 cluster = "gvkey")    # firm-level clustering
summary(iv_main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. OLS baseline (for comparison)
ols_main <- feols(CAR ~ G_index + log_assets + qhat + cash_pct + 
                    leverage + rel_size + tender + stock_pay | 
                    sic2 + year, 
                  cluster = "gvkey", data = data)
summary(ols_main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: use E-index & alternative window CAR[-2,+2]
data <- data %>% mutate(CAR_5d = CAR_2to2)     # assume pre-computed

iv_robust <- feols(CAR_5d ~ 1 | gvkey + year | 
                     (E_index ~ law_CSA + law_BC + law_FP), 
                   data = data, cluster = "gvkey")
summary(iv_robust)
```

======================================================================
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that entrenchment (higher G/E) lowers acquirer shareholders’ gains from acquisitions. Prior event-study evidence suggests average acquirer CARs around 0 % to +1 %. A one-standard-deviation increase in G (≈ 5 provisions) is expected to reduce CAR by roughly 0.5–1.0 percentage points. Hence the IV coefficient θ is predicted to be negative, economically meaningful, and statistically significant.

======================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Strong first-stage (F>10) ………………………………………… 1  
2. Exclusion restriction believable ……………………………… 0.7  
3. No differential pre-trends (tested) …………………………… 0.8  
4. Correct functional form / linearity …………………………… 0.9  
5. Reliable measurement of treatment & outcome ……………… 0.8  

Overall = 4.2 / 5

======================================================================
